analysis:
The PR is documentation-only: docs/reference/protocol-messages.md gains a new section (head lines 202-219) describing the provider's reconnect wait by WebSocket close code. Close code 1012 gets a randomized wait from serviceRestartDelayRange without growing backoff. Any other code, or no close frame, uses the next ExponentialBackoff range. A session open for stableSessionDuration or longer, counted from its register frame, resets the backoff. Every reconnect sends a fresh register. The supplied units are base text only (protocol-messages.md lines 330-955), a heartbeat/capacity/telemetry/inference-message reference. The change region lies outside those base ranges, so I reviewed the patch excerpt plus surrounding context.

Security considerations: the documented behavior (TB-002) only changes reconnect timing and adds no new wire fields, authentication path or decryption path. The close code is read from a coordinator-side frame, and the coordinator is trusted. A network attacker on a TLS-protected channel cannot forge 1012. If one could, the effect would be limited to a short delay without growth, which is bounded by the documented jitter range. The backoff reset after a stable session and the fresh register on every reconnect preserve re-attestation and re-authorization (TB-009, TB-011, T-053). Nothing in the doc suggests that serving authorization or the attestation state survives a reconnect.

The implementation (CoordinatorReconnectPolicy.swift) and the constants (serviceRestartDelayRange, stableSessionDuration) were not supplied, so I cannot verify that they match the doc. If 1012 jitter were too narrow, a thundering-herd reconnect could affect availability, but that is not demonstrable from this evidence. Other base content in the units (add-on busy fields, prefix-cache telemetry, T-041 relevant) is unchanged. No threat-model update is needed beyond the optional note that the reconnect policy is availability-only.
